newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany approves visa rule for foreign children.
newsitem.headline: Germany approves visa rule for foreign children.

text.p: Germany's upper house of parliament approved a ruling requiring visas and residence permits for children from Turkey, Morocco, Tunisia and former Yugoslavia even if they have lived all their lives here.
But it called for streamlined procedures for issuing the documents to up to 800,000 foreign children under 16 who were born here or came as infants with parents seeking work.

The bill cushions the impact of a ruling Interior Minister Manfred Kanther imposed to widespread criticism in January as an emergency measure to stop what he called a wave of children arriving as immigrants, drug couriers or cheap labour.

The Turkish Foreign Ministry promptly issued a statement condemning the bill and calling on the German parliament to "approach the issue on the basis of its human dimension as well as the friendship between the Turkish and German nations."

It asked Bonn to rescind the visa requirement, saying it "will render the human rapprochement between the Turkish and German peoples more difficult" and would create great difficulties for Turkish citizens living here.

Bonn had long waived visa requirements for children under 16 from the four countries now covered by the ruling, which have large minority communities working in Germany, to allow them to visit relatives for up to three months.
But Kanther said parents had abused this loophole sending their children to Germany alone in the hope of securing permanent residence for the whole family.
"This visa policy is about stopping the terrible abuse of children brought into our country," he told parliament, adding the number of minors arriving at German airports alone had soared this year.
Other deputies noted the risk that children visiting could be used for cheap labour, drug smuggling or prostitution because their presence was not registered in Germany.

Many opposition Social Democrats have slammed Kanther's quick move as insensitive and accused him of spreading fear and bitter feelings through the affected communities. They also complained about how long it took to get the documents.

But state officials, who have to house and feed refugees and children arriving alone, supported his general approach. The absence of a visa and residence permit could prevent children from travelling on class trips abroad, for example.
However, they did call for granting automatic citizenship to third-generation foreigners born in Germany.

Last month the European Parliament approved a resolution urging the German government not to require visas of minors as part of a call on European Union countries to renounce any policy that could support racial hatred or xenophobia.
